title: Benchmark report landing page + interactive table review (copy/design)
summary: Team reviewed the benchmark landing page IA and the interactive table UX (filters, metric toggles, export, and disclaimers). Key feedback: clarify what “latency/$” means and how it’s computed; avoid absolute superlatives; add prominent methodology + caveat links; make units and defaults explicit (p50 vs p95, region, context length); and ensure accessibility + mobile behavior is usable. Legal requested tighter comparative language and specific disclaimer placement. Eng confirmed feasibility for CSV/JSON export, “last updated” timestamp, and analytics events, but flagged performance risks if the table loads too many rows by default.
topics: Landing page structure: hero, trust, how we measured, interactive table, CTA
Metric naming: “latency/$” vs “latency per dollar” vs “efficiency score”
Interactive filters: model, region, context length, concurrency/workload preset
Metric toggles: p50/p95 latency, throughput, $/1M tokens, latency/$
Export behavior (CSV/JSON), shareable links, and “last updated” label
Accessibility, mobile layout, and performance (row count, lazy loading)
Analytics events for funnel attribution (filters, exports, CTAs)
questions: Do we show competitor baselines on the interactive table or keep that in the PDF only?
Should the default view be “production mix” workload preset or a neutral baseline (e.g., fixed context length + concurrency=1)?
Can we include streaming metrics (time-to-first-token) without confusing users given our methodology focus?
What’s the minimal disclaimer copy that still satisfies Legal while not scaring off developers?
next_steps: Alicia to revise layout to make methodology + caveats visible above the fold and add clearer units/labels near the table toggles.
Wei/Ethan to rewrite hero + intro copy to define “latency/$” in one sentence and add a short “What this is / what this isn’t” block.
Felix to implement filter defaults + empty states and confirm mobile behavior for the filter drawer.
Tyler to finalize analytics event names and confirm they map to the post-launch KPI dashboard spec.
Michael/Sofia to provide approved disclaimer language and disallowed phrases list for landing page + tooltips.
Jonas/Elliot to provide a short methodology blurb (non-academic) plus a link to the full methodology page.
action_items: Alicia Perez — Update table header area to include: metric definition tooltip, units, and “Last updated” timestamp placement — Due 2025-06-20
Wei Chen — Rewrite disclaimer/tooltips to be scannable (2–3 bullets) and consistent with Legal guidance — Due 2025-06-21
Ethan Wallace — Add a “How to read the table” section with one worked example (model + region) — Due 2025-06-21
Felix Schneider — Add shareable URL state for filters + ensure export button is disabled until data loads — Due 2025-06-24
Tyler Benson — Publish analytics event schema (filter_change, metric_toggle, export_click, cta_click) and owners — Due 2025-06-19
Michael Grant — Provide final approved comparative language + disclaimer placement requirements — Due 2025-06-20
Soojin Lee — Schedule 20-min follow-up review for final copy + legal sign-off checklist — Due 2025-06-21
transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: June 18, 2025
Time: 2:03pm–2:57pm PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Title: Benchmark report landing page + interactive table review (copy/design)
Attendees: Soojin Lee, Ethan Wallace, Alicia Perez, Felix Schneider, Wei Chen, Elliot Price, Henry Cho, Jonas Weber, Michael Grant, Sofia Mendes, Tyler Benson

AUTO SUMMARY (Fireflies)
- Reviewed landing page sections and interactive benchmark table.
- Main edits: define “latency/$”, reduce ambiguity, add disclaimers, avoid over-claiming.
- Confirmed next steps for copy, design, analytics, and legal review.

TRANSCRIPT

[00:00] Soojin Lee: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for jumping. This is the landing page and interactive table review. Goal today is just—make sure the page tells the right story, the table is not confusing, and we’re not creating, like, a legal problem.

[00:18] Alicia Perez: I can share screen. One sec. Okay, you should see Figma. This is the top of the landing page.

[00:26] Ethan Wallace: Yep, seeing it.

[00:28] Alicia Perez: So hero: “Production inference economics benchmark” and then subhead: “latency per dollar across models and regions.” We have a primary CTA “View interactive results” and secondary “Download PDF.” Then we have three tiles: latency, cost, reliability.

[00:45] Michael Grant: Before we go too far—just note on hero language. “Across models and regions” is fine, but we should avoid anything that implies “complete market coverage.” Also avoid “best” or “fastest” in the hero. Keep it descriptive.

[00:58] Soojin Lee: Yeah. We got comments on the earlier draft where we had “the fastest way” and it got redlined.

[01:05] Wei Chen: The other thing is “latency/$” as a symbol—developers like it, but it’s opaque if you’re not already in this world. Can we define it in-line? Like, “Latency per dollar (lower is better)” or whatever the direction is.

[01:17] Jonas Weber: Careful: our metric is an efficiency metric. In the report it’s defined as “latency per dollar” for a standardized workload, so lower is better. But in some internal charts we inverted it. We need consistency.

[01:30] Henry Cho: +1. Also, right now it reads like a single number truth. We should anchor it: “for the production mix workload.” Otherwise someone will run, like, a different context length and go “this is wrong.”

[01:44] Alicia Perez: Okay, so maybe the subhead becomes “Latency per dollar for a standardized production workload. Includes p50/p95 and $/1M tokens.” Something like that.

[01:55] Sofia Mendes: I’d also prefer we avoid “standardized” without saying what it is. “Defined workload” or “published methodology.” Because “standardized” implies an external standard.

[02:06] Ethan Wallace: Right, we can say “defined workload, published methodology.” And then link to the methodology page.

[02:14] Soojin Lee: Can we make the methodology link visible above the fold? That was feedback from the last review.

[02:20] Alicia Perez: Yes. I can add a small line below the subhead: “See methodology” and “View raw data” maybe.

[02:27] Michael Grant: “Raw data” is okay if it’s truly what we’re publishing. If it’s aggregated outputs, call it “results dataset” or “exported results.” Don’t imply we’re publishing everything we logged.

[02:39] Felix Schneider: Engineering-wise the table will consume a versioned JSON that is basically aggregated results by model/region/config. Not the raw logs.

[02:48] Elliot Price: And methodology page will have the “how we measured” summary plus link to GitHub harness and configs. But we’ll keep sensitive IDs out.

[02:58] Tyler Benson: On analytics, if we put “Methodology” above the fold, we should tag clicks. It’s a good signal for serious evaluators.

[03:05] Soojin Lee: Yep. We’ll add an event for that.

[03:10] Alicia Perez: Scrolling. Here’s the interactive table section. You have filters on the left (desktop) and a filter drawer on mobile. Filters: Model, Region, Context length bucket, and Workload preset.

[03:26] Felix Schneider: In the current build we have three presets: “Production mix,” “Prefill-heavy,” “Decode-heavy.” We can add tooltips for what that means.

[03:34] Jonas Weber: Please do. Otherwise people interpret “production mix” as “their production,” which is not necessarily.

[03:40] Wei Chen: The filter labels are a bit jargon-y. Like “prefill” and “decode” — do we want that on a marketing page?

[03:48] Henry Cho: I think the audience is devs, so it’s fine, but tooltips are required. Like “prefill = prompt processing” and “decode = token generation.”

[03:58] Ethan Wallace: Or we can say “Prompt-heavy” / “Generation-heavy” and then in tooltip mention prefill/decode for technical accuracy.

[04:05] Alicia Perez: That might read better.

[04:08] Sofia Mendes: Also “Workload preset” should not look like we are tailoring to win. We should describe it as “workload profiles used in the methodology.”

[04:18] Soojin Lee: Noted. We’ll rename.

[04:21] Alicia Perez: Now the columns. Default columns right now are: Latency/$, p95 latency, throughput tokens/sec, and $/1M tokens. Then there’s a toggle to switch to p50.

[04:34] Wei Chen: p95 default feels right for “production.” But we should label p95 as “p95 end-to-end latency” with units.

[04:42] Jonas Weber: Units are critical. ms, seconds, and for cost it’s dollars per 1M output tokens? Or total tokens?

[04:50] Elliot Price: In the methodology we define $/1M total tokens, where total = input + output, because people pay for both.

[04:57] Ethan Wallace: That needs to be super explicit. Otherwise folks assume “output tokens only” and compare wrong.

[05:03] Michael Grant: Yes, and put the definition in a tooltip. Also, avoid “end-to-end” if we’re not measuring client network. We’re measuring service-side request duration, right?

[05:13] Jonas Weber: Correct. It’s from request accepted to final token (or completion) in the server instrumentation. It does not include client-side overhead.

[05:22] Felix Schneider: We can label it “Server-side latency” and have a small info icon.

[05:27] Alicia Perez: The current design has an “i” icon next to each metric. We can use that for definitions.

[05:33] Tyler Benson: Just keep the hover/click behavior consistent. On mobile, tooltips need to be tap-able, not hover.

[05:39] Alicia Perez: Yep, I’ll ensure that.

[05:42] Soojin Lee: Let’s talk about “latency/$” itself. It’s the headline metric, so it needs a one-sentence definition that’s non-weird.

[05:50] Wei Chen: Proposed: “Latency per dollar estimates how much server time you get for a given spend under the benchmark workload; lower is more efficient.” Something like that.

[06:02] Jonas Weber: It’s not exactly “server time you get,” but it’s okay. The actual definition is (p95 latency) divided by cost per request, normalized to the workload. We should not say “you get.”

[06:12] Ethan Wallace: Maybe: “Latency per dollar combines latency and cost into one efficiency metric for the defined workload. Lower is better.”

[06:20] Michael Grant: That’s good. Add: “Results vary by workload and configuration.”

[06:25] Sofia Mendes: And add “See methodology.” The more we point to the methodology, the safer.

[06:30] Alicia Perez: We can add a small banner right above the table: “These results reflect the benchmark methodology; see details.” with a link.

[06:38] Henry Cho: I like that. Also add “Last updated: <date>” so people know freshness.

[06:44] Felix Schneider: We can render that from the artifact version. It’ll have a build timestamp.

[06:49] Tyler Benson: If “Last updated” is visible, we should also include it in the JSON so it’s consistent.

[06:55] Felix Schneider: Yes.

[06:57] Alicia Perez: Next: export. Right now we have “Export CSV” button top right.

[07:03] Soojin Lee: We promised in the scope export CSV and JSON for web ingestion. Are we exposing JSON publicly?

[07:10] Felix Schneider: We can do “Download CSV” and “Copy JSON URL.” Or just “Export” with two options.

[07:18] Michael Grant: “Copy JSON URL” might expose a stable endpoint that people scrape. Not necessarily a problem, but we should be sure it doesn’t include sensitive fields.

[07:27] Elliot Price: We’ve got redaction and the public schema is safe. But yeah, the URL should be versioned.

[07:34] Jonas Weber: Versioned is key. Otherwise the numbers change and people accuse us of editing.

[07:40] Wei Chen: And if we do versioned, the UI should show “v1.0” or similar.

[07:45] Alicia Perez: Okay, add “Dataset version” near last updated.

[07:50] Tyler Benson: Export click is a strong intent signal. I want that in analytics as “benchmark_export_click” and include export_type.

[07:58] Soojin Lee: Sounds good.

[08:00] Alicia Perez: Now, disclaimers. Currently we have a collapsible “Caveats” accordion below the table.

[08:06] Michael Grant: That is not enough. The key disclaimers need to be visible without a click. Accordions are risky.

[08:13] Sofia Mendes: Agreed. At least a short line like “Benchmarks are estimates; results vary by workload and configuration.” and “Comparisons are based on published methodology.”

[08:23] Ethan Wallace: We can do a two-bullet “Caveats” just under the table header, then “More caveats” accordion below.

[08:30] Alicia Perez: Yes. I can fit two lines above the fold.

[08:35] Henry Cho: Also, we should say what’s included: model version pinned, region list, hardware class. Otherwise people assume we’re changing something.

[08:44] Jonas Weber: We’re pinning model versions, and hardware per region is in the methodology. But I’m hesitant to list hardware on the marketing page because it creates confusion if it’s not uniform.

[08:56] Wei Chen: Could be a tooltip: “Hardware varies by region; see methodology for details.”

[09:01] Jonas Weber: That’s fine.

[09:04] Soojin Lee: What about competitor baselines? Right now the design has a toggle that says “Show external baselines (beta).”

[09:11] Alicia Perez: I left it in as a placeholder. It’s currently off by default.

[09:15] Michael Grant: Strong recommendation: do not ship competitor baseline in the interactive table on day one unless we have extremely tight substantiation and phrasing. Keep it in the PDF with caveats if at all.

[09:28] Sofia Mendes: +1. Interactive comparisons get screenshotted without context.

[09:33] Ethan Wallace: I’m okay dropping it from the landing page and leaving competitor context in the report narrative where we can add footnotes.

[09:40] Henry Cho: From a product transparency perspective, the interactive is meant to be “what you can reproduce on Redwood,” not “market bake-off.”

[09:48] Soojin Lee: Alright. We’ll remove the toggle for public v1. We can keep a private version internally if we need.

[09:56] Felix Schneider: Works for implementation too. Less complexity.

[10:00] Alicia Perez: Next, mobile. Right now on mobile the filters become a bottom sheet. The table itself becomes a stacked card view per row.

[10:09] Wei Chen: Card view is probably required. Tables on mobile are rough.

[10:13] Tyler Benson: If it’s cards, ensure the metric labels repeat. Otherwise people don’t know what the numbers are.

[10:19] Alicia Perez: Yes, each card has “Latency/$”, “p95 latency,” etc.

[10:24] Felix Schneider: Performance note: if we show too many rows, mobile will lag. We should default to top 10 or require at least one filter selection.

[10:34] Jonas Weber: But requiring a filter might feel like gating.

[10:37] Ethan Wallace: What if default is “Recommended view” with a small set: top models + 3 regions. Then you can expand.

[10:44] Henry Cho: Yeah like “Showing curated default view. Adjust filters to see more.”

[10:50] Michael Grant: That’s also safer because it reduces the chance someone misreads a random combination.

[10:56] Soojin Lee: But we need to avoid the appearance of cherry-picking. If we do curated default, we must explain it and let them expand easily.

[11:06] Jonas Weber: You can set the default to “All published models” and “All published regions” but paginate. Like first page 20 rows.

[11:13] Felix Schneider: Pagination or virtualized list. Pagination is simpler and more accessible.

[11:19] Alicia Perez: I can add pagination controls.

[11:22] Wei Chen: And add a “Sort by” dropdown? Right now it auto-sorts by latency/$.

[11:28] Henry Cho: Sorting matters. Users will want to sort by p95, or by $/1M tokens.

[11:34] Felix Schneider: It’s feasible. Sort state should also go into URL.

[11:38] Tyler Benson: And sorting is another analytics event.

[11:41] Soojin Lee: Let’s not explode scope. Minimum: default sort by latency/$, allow sort by the other three metrics.

[11:49] Alicia Perez: Okay.

[11:51] Ethan Wallace: Can we also include a “How to read this” section? People will land, see numbers, bounce.

[11:57] Wei Chen: I drafted something but it’s too long. Maybe a short block with an example.

[12:03] Jonas Weber: Example should not be a claim. Just a walkthrough like “Pick region X, model Y, look at p95 and $/1M.”

[12:11] Michael Grant: Right. Avoid “We’re 2x better” type example.

[12:16] Alicia Perez: Layout wise, we can add a right rail on desktop with “How to read” and “FAQ.”

[12:22] Henry Cho: FAQ should include: “Can I reproduce this?” and “Does caching affect the results?” Those come up.

[12:30] Elliot Price: On caching: we’re using a defined caching/batching policy. We should say it’s representative of production, not a special one-off.

[12:39] Jonas Weber: Specifically: caching is enabled where applicable, but we control warmup and avoid cross-run contamination. Need careful wording.

[12:48] Wei Chen: We can say: “Caching and batching are configured per methodology; details in the methodology section.”

[12:55] Sofia Mendes: Yes, avoid implying we used “secret sauce” settings that customers can’t access.

[13:01] Soojin Lee: Great. Let’s keep going. Alicia, scroll further down.

[13:05] Alicia Perez: Below the table we have “Key takeaways” and then “Methodology highlights.” The methodology highlights are three bullets: workload definition, regions, stability checks.

[13:16] Jonas Weber: Add “repeat runs / variance” callout. That helps credibility.

[13:21] Ethan Wallace: And maybe “p95 variance thresholds” but simplified.

[13:25] Michael Grant: “Stability checks” is good; it’s not a claim, it’s process.

[13:30] Tyler Benson: Also we need a CTA section at the bottom: trial vs talk to sales. Right now it’s only “Start for free.”

[13:38] Soojin Lee: Good point. We need dual CTA: Hosted signups and Dedicated/Private contact.

[13:44] Henry Cho: We can route based on intent: if they export or they view methodology, show “Talk to an engineer.”

[13:51] Tyler Benson: Personalization is a bigger project, but we can at least track and retarget.

[13:56] Felix Schneider: Implementing conditional CTAs on first version is doable, but we’ll need design sign-off.

[14:03] Alicia Perez: I can add a second CTA: “Get Dedicated sizing” or “Book a demo.”

[14:09] Ethan Wallace: “Get Dedicated sizing” is nice and specific.

[14:12] Sofia Mendes: Just be careful not to imply the benchmark equals a guarantee. “Sizing guidance” is fine.

[14:18] Soojin Lee: Okay.

[14:20] Wei Chen: One more copy thing: “reliability” tile in the hero. We’re not benchmarking reliability on this page. We have some SLO language but it’s not in the dataset.

[14:30] Henry Cho: Yeah, reliability is part of the narrative but not measured in the same table.

[14:36] Ethan Wallace: We can say “Operational consistency” and keep it as a pillar with supporting text: “repeatable performance across regions; stability gates.” That is closer to what we did.

[14:45] Jonas Weber: Yes, that’s accurate.

[14:48] Michael Grant: Just avoid “guaranteed” and “always.”

[14:52] Alicia Perez: I’ll update the tile labels.

[14:55] Soojin Lee: Can we talk through the disclaimers placement one more time, Michael/Sofia? What do you need above the fold.

[15:02] Michael Grant: Minimum: (1) results are based on published methodology and defined workloads; (2) results vary by workload/config/traffic; (3) definitions for what the latency measurement includes/excludes (server-side). If we mention comparisons at all, we need “not an endorsement” etc. But we’re removing competitor toggle, so less.

[15:21] Sofia Mendes: Also, if we use “production” in the headline, qualify it. “Representative production mix” rather than “your production.”

[15:29] Wei Chen: That’s a good point. “Production mix” might be interpreted as universal.

[15:34] Jonas Weber: We called it prompt set v3 production mix internally, but on the page we can call it “Representative mix.”

[15:41] Henry Cho: But keep the technical anchor somewhere for folks who want to map it to the repo.

[15:46] Elliot Price: Methodology page can say “Prompt set v3 (representative production mix).”

[15:51] Soojin Lee: Great.

[15:53] Felix Schneider: Quick technical note: shareable links. If we store filter state in URL query params, we must be careful with length. But it’s fine.

[16:01] Tyler Benson: Query params are great for attribution too.

[16:05] Alicia Perez: In the design, we can add “Share” button or just rely on URL.

[16:10] Ethan Wallace: Let’s not add a button unless we need it. Keep it simple.

[16:14] Soojin Lee: Agreed.

[16:16] Alicia Perez: Anything else on table? I want to cover chart styling too. We have small sparklines for latency distribution as a mini bar.

[16:25] Jonas Weber: Distribution charts might be too much. Unless we’re showing p50/p95 only, distribution will create questions.

[16:32] Henry Cho: I’d remove sparklines for v1. Keep it numeric. Add a future enhancement.

[16:38] Michael Grant: Yes, distribution implies we’re publishing full distribution data; we may not be.

[16:44] Felix Schneider: We are not exposing full histograms publicly right now. So better to avoid.

[16:49] Alicia Perez: Okay, removing sparklines.

[16:52] Wei Chen: On the metric labels, do we use “tokens/sec” or “tok/s”? Developer-friendly is “tok/s” but clarity is “tokens/sec.”

[16:59] Ethan Wallace: Use “tokens/s.”

[17:02] Henry Cho: And specify whether it’s output tokens/s or total tokens/s.

[17:07] Jonas Weber: We compute throughput as output tokens per second in decode phase plus prefill? Actually our metric is effective tokens/s across total tokens. This is exactly why it’s tricky.

[17:17] Felix Schneider: In the dataset we have “effective_tokens_per_s” which is total tokens / total time.

[17:23] Jonas Weber: Then label as “Effective tokens/s (input+output).” with tooltip.

[17:30] Wei Chen: Great. That will prevent confusion.

[17:33] Tyler Benson: Please keep the tooltips short. People don’t read novels.

[17:38] Alicia Perez: Understood.

[17:40] Soojin Lee: Okay, let’s do a quick round: what are the top edits we need before we can say the page is in ‘content freeze’?

[17:48] Ethan Wallace: For me: hero rewrite with clear definition; “How to read” section; remove competitor toggle; add visible caveats; and update the reliability pillar language.

[18:00] Wei Chen: Add units everywhere, make server-side latency explicit, and make $/1M token definition explicit.

[18:07] Alicia Perez: Design: disclaimers above fold, pagination and sorting controls, mobile filter drawer clarity.

[18:14] Felix Schneider: Implementation: sort + pagination + URL state, export behavior, and “last updated/version.”

[18:22] Tyler Benson: Analytics: methodology clicks, filter changes, sort changes, export, and CTA clicks. And ensure the events have consistent names.

[18:30] Michael Grant: Legal: approved disclaimer copy and a final pass on any comparative phrasing.

[18:36] Sofia Mendes: And ensure we’re not implying completeness or guarantees.

[18:41] Soojin Lee: Great. I’ll send a recap with owners.

[18:45] (crosstalk)

[18:46] Henry Cho: One last thing—can we add a small note about “supported vs experimental” regions? Product thread had concerns.

[18:53] Soojin Lee: Good catch. We can label regions as “Published” and hide “experimental” from public.

[18:59] Felix Schneider: I can filter the dataset to only include published regions.

[19:03] Jonas Weber: That’s aligned with methodology anyway.

[19:06] Soojin Lee: Okay.

[19:08] Alicia Perez: Are we good? I’ll take these and update the Figma by Friday.

[19:12] Soojin Lee: Perfect. Next review: short 20 minutes once copy is in and legal has the disclaimer text.

[19:19] Michael Grant: Please route the final draft through me and Sofia before it goes to PR merge.

[19:24] Wei Chen: Will do.

[19:26] Soojin Lee: Thanks all.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling / wrap-up chatter; recording ends.)
